fields.title: Relational Databases: Rigidity as a Guarantee
fields.keyTakeaway: A relational database trades flexibility for guarantees: data that cannot afford mistakes lives here.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Why do most products handling money run on a relational database under the hood — and why is this a deliberate choice rather than inertia?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A PM for whom "database" is a single thing doesn't understand the phrase "let's put this in Redis" and cannot participate in conversations deciding whether a feature will be fast. They also don't understand when an engineer says "this data can drift" — treating the warning as overcautiousness until they see a discrepancy in production.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: A [[relational-database|relational database]] stores data in tables. A row is a record, a column is an attribute. All rows in a table have the same set of columns; this is the [[schema|schema]], and the database enforces it.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: Three consequences important for the product.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **The database refuses to accept incorrect data.** If an order requires a user, the database won't let you create an orphan order — even if the code asks. This is protection against programmer errors at the storage level, meaning data is generally trustworthy.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Relations are enforced at the storage level.** You cannot delete a user and leave hanging orders. The database will either block it or cascade delete, but it won't leave garbage. For the product, this means "delete account" is a predictable operation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Data can be joined arbitrarily.** The [[sql|SQL]] language allows assembling any report from any tables, even if such a query wasn't planned during design. "How many orders were placed by users who registered in March in stores with a rating above four" is a single query, not a project.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The price for this is rigidity. Changing the schema requires a [[migration|migration]], and migrating a large table costs time and risk.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Orders, payments, and stock in a relational database. The reason is not tradition, but a specific property: an order and money deduction must always be consistent, not "eventually." If money was deducted but the order wasn't created, that is an unrecoverable situation involving a real user and real money.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The flip side showed up when the product wanted to store product specifications. Milk has fat content and volume, laundry detergent has weight and load type, bananas have nothing. In a relational model, this is either a table with a hundred mostly empty columns, or a separate "product attribute" table with name-value pairs, where filtering becomes slow and awkward. Neither option is good, and that's the right moment to consider a different datastore specifically for the catalog.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Schema rigidity costs dearly when changes are frequent: an early-stage product where the model changes weekly may suffer from it. And relational databases scale harder than non-relational ones — up to certain volumes it doesn't matter, after that it does.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A relational database trades flexibility for guarantees: data that cannot afford mistakes lives here.
